papers.title: SituRecBench: Evaluating Frontier Models as Situated Recommendation Assistants in 3D Environments
papers.abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.

papers.title: Track or Follow? A Jev-Compatible Multi-Agent Trading System When Web News Lags the Market
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly trade on the Web news they read, yet much Web news about listed firms is published after, and about, the price move it reports, so a reader can agree with the market by following it instead of reading the event. We ask whether LLM judgments of Web news track the market's reaction to the reported event or follow it. To answer, we built a multi-agent trading system whose agents share only point-in-time stores and answer typed questions through the interface of Jev, a hosted typed decision model; code sets every position under a proved bound on how far text can move it. In a hash-committed test of a Jev-compatible reader built from a pinned LLM's option probabilities, item judgments track announcement-window abnormal returns (weekly Spearman 0.119), also after the LLM's release, and event types agree with the issuers' 8-K filings (AUC 0.833); Jev's judgments of news published after its own release track the reaction as well (descriptive). Exploratory analyses show where the association comes from: 72% of earnings news items appear after the issuer's filing, contributor-written items often report the price move, and from the first trade after publication the association falls to 0.023. At a weekly horizon, the confirmatory test detects no rank information over code-only features. Under attack, decision cards traced 88% of successful attacks to the planted item. We propose that market-graded tests of Web-text readers report the criterion from publication, not only from the event.

papers.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
papers.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems face two costs that research comparisons rarely measure: building the graph, and removing documents from it. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions carrying chunk-level provenance. Indexing makes one language-model call per passage, retrieval makes none, and deleting a document is a database operation with no model calls. On the full 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus we verify that, after deleting 10% of the documents, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. We compare Lightfoot with HippoRAG 2, LightRAG and fast-graphrag under identical extraction, answer and embedding models on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA. Lightfoot builds the cheapest index on all three datasets, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2 and 3-6x below LightRAG and fast-graphrag. Against HippoRAG 2 it is significantly better on MuSiQue retrieval (+2.8 points recall@5 and +4.3 recall@10 on a held-out split) and on HotpotQA answers (+7.7 points exact match), and significantly worse on 2WikiMultiHopQA (-3.9 recall@2, -8.4 F1). Deleting the same documents took LightRAG 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours; fast-graphrag has no deletion path. Code and per-question results: https://github.com/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG

papers.title: Search-by-Answer Bias in Retrieval Models
papers.abstract: Dense retrievers are meant to select passages that match a query's semantic specification. We show they suffer from search-by-answer bias: they favor passages that mention answer objects the model knows (scores as likely), over passages that support valid alternative answers. We test this with controlled factual contrasts from LAMA/TREx. For each retriever, we measure how strongly the model scores the canonical object over an alternative object using a token-prediction head, and ask whether this score predicts passage rankings. Across eight retrievers, including DPR, Spider variants, Contriever, E5, and Qwen3-Embedding, larger token-prediction scores consistently predict higher retrieval scores for passages containing the corresponding object. This holds when passages differ only in the answer object, and even when the passage that mentions the high-scoring object expresses a wrong relation. Dense retrieval thus exhibits search-by-answer bias during passage selection, shaping which evidence is retrieved.

papers.title: Hidden Distances: How Likert-Scale Spacing Shapes Algorithmic Voting Advice
papers.abstract: Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) are algorithmic recommenders that match voters with political candidates on policy preferences. They are widely adopted across many multi-party democracies; in Denmark, 62\% of eligible voters used a VAA ahead of the 2022 general election, and 45\% of VAA users reported following its advice. VAAs typically ask voters and candidates to respond to policy statements on a Likert scale, from ``strongly disagree'' to ``strongly agree'', and recommend candidates whose responses are closest to the voter's. Computing these distances requires assigning numbers to response options, a design choice without an empirical basis, since it is unknown how people perceive the distances between options. Here we show that this seemingly technical choice substantially changes whom voters are matched with. We parameterize the distance between ``(dis)agree'' and ``strongly (dis)agree'' relative to the distance between ``neutral'' and ``(dis)agree'' as $\alpha$, and quantify how it changes recommendations for a popular Danish VAA. We find that moving from equidistant options to doubling this distance can change $37.7\%$ of top candidate matches and $21.9\%$ of top party matches, although no answers change. Low $\alpha$-values favor candidates with strong positions, with some parties receiving up to $ 19.6\%$ more recommendations, while high $\alpha$-values favor moderates. Similarly, female candidates receive fewer recommendations at low $\alpha$ and more at high $\alpha$-values. Our findings demonstrate that undisclosed quantification choices in algorithmic recommenders can carry considerable electoral consequences, and they call for transparency and sensitivity analysis in VAA design. As Likert-based matching also underpins dating platforms and roommate allocation systems, these implications extend well beyond elections.

papers.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. \textsc{NarrativeBench} provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.

papers.title: DM-Call: Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling with Cumulative Verification Feedback
papers.abstract: Reliable function calling requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to select appropriate functions and generate arguments consistent with user intent. However, syntactically valid calls may still be semantically incorrect due to inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments. In this paper, we propose Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that combines local schema validation with separate decision-model verification of function selection and argument correctness. For rejected candidates, DM-Call accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across attempts. A hybrid feedback representation further combines numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels to guide iterative refinement without executing external tools. Extensive evaluation across BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) demonstrates DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy versus direct generation, at modest additional cost.

papers.title: Slim Foundation Models for Latency-Critical Recommendation Serving
papers.abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a core component of recommendation and advertising systems. Large language models (LLMs) offer rich semantic priors that improve prediction quality, particularly in cold-start and long-tail settings. Injecting a full-scale LLM into a CTR pipeline is, however, prohibitively expensive at inference time: existing LLM-enhanced CTR methods avoid this cost by caching LLM outputs offline rather than serving the LLM online. We propose a resource-efficient pipeline, SlimFM, that makes online LLM-based semantic modeling practical: (1) dependency-aware structured pruning compresses LLaMA3-8B by 44% to a 4.5B-parameter backbone; (2) LoRA-based field-aware fine-tuning trains the pruned model to produce discriminative field-level semantic embeddings from lightweight textual prompts; (3) a semantic-guided fusion module injects these embeddings into the feature interactions of a conventional CTR model. Across four datasets and six CTR backbones, SlimFM retains over 99% of uncompressed-model accuracy while reducing inference latency by up to 3.4x relative to existing LLM-enhanced baselines.

papers.title: Hybrid Product Search Without the Copy: Lexical, Semantic and Filtered Retrieval Served Directly from a Data Lake
papers.abstract: E-commerce catalogs increasingly live in lakehouse tables: Apache Iceberg metadata over Parquet files in object storage. Product search, however, still runs on copies of that catalog, in a lexical engine and a vector database, each with its own ingestion pipeline, schema, staleness window and bill. We show that search applications can be hosted directly on the data lake, with the lakehouse table as the single system of record. We extend Apache Pinot, a real-time OLAP engine that already serves Iceberg tables in place, with BM25 relevance scoring over its Lucene text index, corpus-wide term statistics so that scores are comparable across files, and reciprocal rank fusion in plain SQL; a real-time table fed by a stream can sit behind the same table, merged by the broker. On the Amazon ESCI benchmark (1.2M US products, 22,458 test queries), hybrid search served from the lake matches exact retrieval (nDCG@10 .361). The lake table is queryable 149 s after its files are registered, and a lake commit is searchable in 3.8 s, close to indexing directly into a search engine. On a brand-sorted lake of 277M products (0.8 TB), one 16-vCPU node answers brand-scoped vector, BM25 and client-fused hybrid searches in 6.5-9 ms (p50), sustains 1,100 vector and 635 BM25 searches per second at under 180 ms p99, and makes a commit searchable in 4.3 s. Search adds only its indexes: no copy of the catalog, no sync pipeline and no second schema, which cuts storage, rebuild time and the operational work of keeping copies consistent.

papers.title: Dhara: Evidence-Oriented Retrieval for Indian Knowledge Systems
papers.abstract: Relevant evidence in Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS) collections may be distributed across passages in different parts of a work, including verses, translations, and commentaries. Locating it requires matching natural-language questions and partially remembered verse fragments to source passages. We present Dhara, a retrieval engine combining hybrid search, chapter- and book-level Entity Notes (EN), Fuzzy Verse Retrieval (FVR), and neural reranking. Five comparisons on the 325 questions in Dhara Bench examine retrieval representations against BM25, EN's contribution, reranker quality and computation time, FVR, and Gemini. BGE-M3 single-vector retrieval exceeds BM25 in nDCG@10, Recall@20, and MRR@20 across all categories. Its scores are broadly comparable to ColBERTv2, with mean retrieval times of 0.108 s and 0.962 s under the same hardware configuration and a smaller memory footprint for chunk storage on disk. Adding EN to a direct branch with a matched candidate count improves nDCG@10 in all twelve categories with Qwen and ten with BGE; the combined ranking is capped at the same candidate count. Qwen improves nDCG@10, Precision@5, and MRR@20 over BGE in every category, at approximately 6.72 times the overall estimated serial computation time. FVR increases Verse-category nDCG@10 by approximately 20 percentage points with either reranker. Gemini is evaluated after source mapping and manual review with relevance annotations visible. The Qwen pipeline with EN and FVR has higher Recall@20 than Gemini in ten categories and stronger complete-evidence retrieval in Multi-hop questions, while Gemini retains early-relevance advantages in several categories. The results inform retrieval choices according to evidence requirements and resource budgets.

papers.title: CHO-Bench: How Do Context Hints Affect Ad Rankings in LLM Advertising?
papers.abstract: LLM advertising selects advertisements based on user conversations, where user needs may extend beyond explicit product searches. ChatGPT Ads allows advertisers to provide natural-language context hints describing what they offer, who may find it useful, and when it may be useful, as additional information for ranking advertisements across diverse user conversations. However, how to effectively construct these hints remains unclear. We formulate Context Hint Optimization (CHO) as the problem of constructing context hints to improve an advertisement's ranking under a given budget. Drawing on established marketing frameworks, we develop seven context hint generation strategies covering What, Who, and When, along with a Unified strategy that combines all seven dimensions. We introduce CHO-Bench and conduct over 1.19 million paired evaluations across five datasets using embedding-based and LLM-based rankers. Our results show that context hints improve advertisement rankings under the evaluated offline rankers. While individual strategies achieve similar average gains and Unified offers no consistent advantage, strategy differences become more pronounced under specific generation-ranking configurations, with embedding-based and LLM-based rankers favoring different information dimensions. Increasing the hint budget further improves rankings with diminishing marginal gains. These findings establish an offline benchmark for studying ad-side ranking optimization in LLM advertising and highlight opportunities for model-specific hint selection and budget-aware generation and aggregation.

papers.title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
papers.abstract: On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.

papers.title: RecoGEM: A Serving System for Production-Scale Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) is moving industrial recommender systems (RecSys) from scoring candidate items to autoregressively generating item identifiers. This shift promises higher recommendation quality, but makes serving substantially harder: each request executes a short sequence of dependent decoding steps that explore a large item space and select promising candidates on the latency-critical path. GR not only creates structural mismatches with conventional RecSys pipelines, but also challenges the architectural and optimization assumptions of LLM serving stacks, making direct adoption of existing systems difficult. We present RecoGEM, our production GR serving system. RecoGEM uses a runtime--engine decoupling architecture to move GR-specific serving responsibilities, such as candidate-state transitions and live artifact updates, to a dedicated runtime. Its execution engine exploits GR's short token sequences, large candidate populations, and predictable step shapes to optimize self-attention, candidate selection, and execution planning. RecoGEM has been deployed for over nine months across our production lines, serving applications with hundreds of millions of users and supporting more than ten GR model families. On our OneModel production workloads, RecoGEM reaches over 1,000 QPS per serving instance with P99 latency below 35 ms and a 2.88$\times$ throughput improvement over representative baselines.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
papers.abstract: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.

papers.title: JU\'A -- A Benchmark for Information Retrieval in Brazilian Legal Text Collections
papers.abstract: Legal information retrieval in Portuguese remains difficult to evaluate systematically because available datasets differ widely in document type, query style, and relevance definition. We present JU\'A, a public benchmark for Brazilian legal retrieval designed to support more reproducible and comparable evaluation across heterogeneous legal collections. More broadly, JU\'A is intended not only as a benchmark, but as a continuous evaluation infrastructure for Brazilian legal IR, combining shared protocols, common ranking metrics, fixed splits when applicable, and a public leaderboard. The benchmark covers jurisprudence retrieval as well as broader legislative, regulatory, and question-driven legal search. We evaluate lexical, dense, and BM25-based reranking pipelines, including a domain-adapted Qwen embedding model fine-tuned on JU\'A-aligned supervision. Results show that the benchmark is sufficiently heterogeneous to distinguish retrieval paradigms and reveal substantial cross-dataset trade-offs. Domain adaptation yields its clearest gains on the supervision-aligned JU\'A-Juris subset, while BM25 remains highly competitive on other collections, especially in settings with strong lexical and institutional phrasing cues. Overall, JU\'A provides a practical evaluation framework for studying legal retrieval across multiple Brazilian legal domains under a common benchmark design.

papers.title: An Embarrassingly Simple Graph Heuristic Reveals Shortcut-Solvable Benchmarks for Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation has increasingly shifted toward generative recommenders that combine sequential patterns with semantic item information. Yet these methods are often evaluated on a small set of widely used benchmarks, raising a key question: do these benchmarks actually require the advanced modeling capabilities that modern generative recommenders claim to provide? We conduct a benchmark audit with an intentionally simple graph heuristic. Starting from only the last one or two interacted items, it retrieves candidates from a few-hop item-transition graph and ranks them by item-feature similarity. Despite using no sequence encoder, generative objective, or training, this heuristic matches or outperforms many modern baselines, with relative NDCG@10 improvements of 38.10% and 44.18% over the best competing baseline on Amazon Review Sports and CDs. We show that this behavior reflects shortcut solvability rather than an artifact of one heuristic. We identify three shortcut structures that can make next-item prediction easier than expected: low-branching local transitions, feature-smooth transitions, and limited dependence on long user histories. These shortcuts need not appear together; even one or two strong signals can make simple local retrieval highly competitive, while weakening them makes the benefits of more sophisticated models clearer. Across 14 datasets, model rankings vary substantially with dataset properties, yet the heuristic remains competitive on 10 of them. Our findings suggest that strong performance on standard benchmarks does not always demonstrate advanced sequential, semantic, or generative modeling ability. We call for more careful dataset selection and dataset-level diagnostic analysis when using benchmarks to support claims about new recommendation models.

papers.title: VEX-Bench: Benchmarking Verification Complexity of LLM-Generated Misinformation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made misinformation inexpensive to produce but not to verify, creating a growing asymmetry in the information ecosystem. Under tight time, labor, and budget constraints, media organizations, platforms, and fact-checkers rely on screening to prioritize which content to verify. We introduce VEX-Bench, a unified benchmark for evaluating the verification complexity of LLM-generated misinformation, as perceived during screening, across models and generation methods. Verification complexity is assessed along multiple dimensions derived from journalistic and fact-checking practices, capturing checkability, harm potential, source credibility signals, imposter legitimacy, and expected verification effort. We define the VEX score as an integrated measure combining elicitation yield and verification complexity to quantify how generated content consumes limited verification capacity. We construct a benchmark spanning two misinformation categories, 6 high-stakes domains, and 60 real-world topics, and evaluate 7 frontier LLMs and 7 generation methods, yielding 5{,}880 articles. We employ an LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation and validate it using content-analysis methodology, including ordinal Krippendorff $\alpha$ for inter-annotator reliability, complemented by fact-checking agents for verification. Our findings show that no single method dominates all dimensions, underscoring the need for multi-dimensional evaluation. LLMs can generate high-VEX misinformation at 3$\times$ to 169$\times$ lower cost than agent-based verification. Such content is often prioritized during screening, consuming scarce verification resources and introducing a systematic risk of misallocation in resource-constrained verification systems. The code is publicly available in our \href{https://github.com/HanxunH/VEX-Bench}{GitHub repository}.

papers.title: Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence
papers.abstract: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve evidence from stored conversations and documents to answer queries. Most embedding-based retrievers compare single-vector representations of queries and memories, even when relevance depends on a small part of the content. Such local evidence can be matched to queries using the contextual token representations already computed by the same embedding models. Our method uses sparse token matching to improve retrieval without additional training. Each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories. The matching scores are aggregated for each memory and combined with whole-memory similarity to rank memories. An optional low-rank query adapter can be trained with supervision while keeping the encoder and stored memory representations fixed. Our method improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families without additional training. Query adaptation further increases the gains to 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B. These retrieval gains translate into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.

papers.title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
papers.abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.

papers.title: Dhara Bench: An Evidence-Oriented Retrieval Benchmark for Indian Knowledge Systems
papers.abstract: Dhara Bench is a retrieval benchmark for Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS), with 325 questions in 12 categories and 60,121 text chunks from 15 source groups. The categories were developed based on 4,500 questions submitted to the Dhara application; the evaluation set combines corpus-aligned application queries with expert-contributed questions. The annotations comprise 7,578 question-chunk relevance links involving 6,847 distinct corpus chunks. For 34 composite and multi-hop questions, 401 conjugate groups specify alternative sets of passages that jointly support each question. Chunk identifiers and hierarchical references connect the judgments to their source texts. The paper describes corpus preparation, annotation, and validation, and reports a fixed BM25 baseline implemented with Pyserini with $k_1=0.9$ and $b=0.4$. Across all questions, BM25 achieves MRR@20 of 0.315, Recall@10 of 0.182, and nDCG@10 of 0.205. On the group-annotated subset, complete-evidence scores are CE_Recall@20 = 0.294 and CE_MRR@20 = 0.141. The category results expose particularly weak verse retrieval, while group scores reveal gaps between finding individual passages and completing their support. The corpus and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/Avinash2236/Dhara-Bench.

papers.title: Close and Sort: Exact Maximum-Likelihood Aggregation of Cyclic Rank-Two Preferences
papers.abstract: Pairwise probabilities arise in rank aggregation, recommendation, and human or LLM evaluation, yet converting them into a maximum-likelihood list is a weighted Kemeny problem and is NP-hard in general. Known exact algorithms for rank-two tournaments use only comparison signs and do not optimize this likelihood. We show that the weighted problem is exactly solvable when the skew-symmetric log-odds matrix $W_{ij}=\log(p_{ij}/p_{ji})$ has rank two, including when the induced preferences contain cycles. Writing $W_{ij}=\det(h_i,h_j)$ and adding the closing vector $h_0=-\sum_i h_i$ turns the objective into twice the signed area of a closed polygon. This geometry yields CloseSort, which polar-sorts the $n+1$ edge vectors, cuts after $h_0$, and returns a global maximum-likelihood order in $O(n\log n)$ time from the factors. The same geometry identifies the runner-up and gives a stability certificate beyond exact rank two. When the smallest determinant $\delta$ of two consecutive edges in the closed angular cycle is positive, it is exactly the best-to-runner-up log-likelihood gap. For $W=W_0+E$, the CloseSort order of $W_0$ has regret at most $\sum_{i<j}|E_{ij}|$ on $W$ and remains optimal whenever this sum is below $\delta$, a worst-case tight threshold. In 5,120 determinant-logit simulations, increasing the observations per pair from 4 to 64 raises the fraction on which rank-two projection outperforms the empirical plug-in optimum from 68.6% to 85.7%. On 3,600 Arena-Hard LLM-judge profiles drawn from 63 systems and ten judges, the leading rank-two component captures 89.2% of the log-odds energy. On profiles containing a directed majority triangle, CloseSort reduces normalized regret by 44% relative to Borda and improves the mean normalized objective over each of eight baselines. With factors supplied, it is 8,407 times faster than exact dynamic programming on 18-item rankings.

papers.title: MapHub: Daily Relevance Heatmaps of New arXiv Preprints for a Research Community
papers.abstract: MapHub, the MIDAS arXiv Preprint Hub, assesses each day's new arXiv submissions for every participant in a research community, with a large language model reading each paper against portfolios built for the participants. It publishes the relevance scores, from 0 to 100, as a heatmap that shows whose work each paper touches. In the authors' blind ratings, the top 10\% of papers by MapHub's scores held about 70\% of the raters' own top 5\%, pooled, against about a third for a text-matching baseline. About 6\% of a day's astro-ph papers reach 30 for each participant, and one every three days reaches 60. MapHub runs on a standard Claude subscription and is designed to be useful for any field: https://github.com/kailicao/maphub-public

papers.title: Edge-Deployable LLMs for Classification and Value-of-Information Ranking of Disaster-Related Tweets
papers.abstract: Humanitarian-aid and disaster relief decisions often rely on noisy, incomplete, and uncertain information from social media. Although substantial research has focused on automating the classification of such data, limited work has examined whether individual posts contain sufficient information to support decisions to act. In this study, we use large language models (LLMs) to (1) classify social media content and (2) assess its Value-of-Information (VoI) in terms of operational actionability. We evaluate seven LLMs for the classification of 77,484 tweets across 10 humanitarian-aid categories and identify the Qwen3 (8B parameters) model as the top-performing classifier, achieving the highest F1 scores in all but one category. In a second task, the classified categories serve as contextual inputs for assessing VoI with respect to responder actionability across six well established metrics for each tweet. We observed that the Gemma 3 (4B parameters) model outperformed the other models on this task, achieving the highest recall across the majority of categories. This work demonstrates that relatively small, edge-deployable LLMs can prioritize actionable information in resource-constrained environments. By integrating VoI assessment, our framework advances the automated elicitation of high-utility knowledge from unstructured social media streams for disaster-response decision-making and highlights a pathway toward tactical edge applications using LLMs that fit on a single 8 GB GPU.

papers.title: SepLRM: A Foundation Model Paradigm for Recommendation
papers.abstract: Large recommendation models (LRMs) improve recommendation performance by scaling behavior sequence length, model capacity, and training compute. However, the return on investment (ROI) of continued scaling deteriorates as marginal gains diminish and long-sequence encoding costs rise, especially when this computation is repeatedly executed by distinct models for diverse recommendation stages and business scenarios. To address this issue, we propose SepLRM, a recommendation foundation model (RFM) paradigm that identifies reusable sequence encoding and reorganizes multiple end-to-end (E2E) LRMs into one RFM and multiple independently optimized vertical models (VMs). The RFM adopts an encoder-decoder architecture and exports its final-layer encoder state as the shared key-value (KV) cache that is independent of downstream task-offered candidates. Unlike candidate-specific logits or aggregated user embeddings, the KV cache preserves fine-grained behavioral information. Separation at this native KV interface also allows each VM to construct candidate-conditioned queries while retaining the same query-KV interaction as its E2E counterpart, enabling high-fidelity capability transfer. To ensure both transfer effectiveness and system efficiency, we co-design cache compression, the training and serving workflows, and LG-Store, a distributed storage system for KV caches. Experiments on three large-scale datasets show that SepLRM achieves state-of-the-art offline performance with a transfer rate of approximately 100%. It also demonstrates strong transferability across model iterations, recommendation stages, and business scenarios. Deployment in two large-scale industrial scenarios substantially improves the ROI of sequence scaling and delivers consistent gains in online A/B tests at ByteDance.

papers.title: LEGIT: Live Eligibility Gating over Identifier Tries for Constrained Decoding of Heterogeneous Pages
papers.abstract: A generative recommender names each candidate with a short token sequence, a Semantic ID, and recommends by generating those tokens. Some generative recommenders, including the Uber Eats search engine we are building, write a whole results page, stores with their menu items, in one decoding pass. Every Semantic ID on such a page must name a real store or item that is eligible for the search, such as a store that delivers to the user's location, and that is not already on the page. Each item must also belong to the store above it. A trie over the catalog keeps identifiers real, but eligibility and repetition change with every request and token, and the grammar-constrained decoder we tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly. We call this constraint LEGIT, for live eligibility gating over identifier tries. Numbering trie leaves depth first turns each rule into a range lookup over one store trie and one item trie, and every generated page passes an independent catalog check. On one NVIDIA B200 GPU with one or two requests per decode step, a direct implementation that walks the trie on the GPU makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding. Across 36 implementations, hardware counters and ablations are consistent with kernel launches and CPU-GPU waits as the source of this slowdown. Our fastest implementation walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model, needs no custom kernel, and cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against the direct GPU implementation, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost. This implementation is also the fastest on a page layout that puts each item before its store.

papers.title: Yuanbao-Reranker: Document-Grounded Synthesis and Preference Distillation for Text Reranking
papers.abstract: High-precision text reranking is a critical component in modern search, recommendation, and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. We present Yuanbao-Reranker, a family of general-purpose dense rerankers spanning 0.6B, 4B, and 8B parameter scales built upon the Qwen3 backbone. To construct diverse and reliable ranking supervision at scale, we pair answer-first and query-type-guided document-grounded synthesis with a three-stage curation funnel that verifies positive support, eliminates semantic redundancy, and enforces balanced source-by-length quotas. For each curated pair, we screen real retrieval pools with a teacher score margin to filter out potential false negatives and sample Hard, Medium, and Moderate negative tiers, yielding 2.75M $1{:}3$ ranking groups. We train the models by jointly optimizing pointwise relevance cross-entropy and a bounded minimum-gap hinge objective over both positive--negative and negative--negative pairs. This formulation transfers fine-grained teacher preferences across candidate tiers without over-constraining well-separated predictions, supporting both cross-scale and same-scale distillation followed by layerwise adaptive model merging. Across five comprehensive benchmarks spanning Chinese (CMTEB-R), multilingual (MMTEB-R), English (BEIR), long-document (MLDR), and code (MTEB-Code) retrieval, Yuanbao-Reranker consistently leads every parameter tier: the 0.6B variant reaches 70.96 Avg. to surpass 1B--4B active-parameter baselines, the 4B variant reaches 73.63 Avg. to outperform the 8B teacher (72.68), and the 8B variant achieves a state-of-the-art 74.21 Avg., with substantial gains generalizing across distinct first-stage retrievers.

papers.title: When Greedy Is Sorting: Exact and Certified Ideal Rankings for Novelty Metrics
papers.abstract: The ideal ranking that normalizes novelty metrics is NP-hard to compute in general, so widely used $\alpha$-nDCG evaluators approximate its denominator with a greedy rule that rescans every remaining document at each rank. We identify a regime in which this ideal ranking is exact and cheap for both $\alpha$-DCG and intent-aware expected reciprocal rank (ERR-IA). When each document is positively judged for at most one intent, each metric reduces to the classical allocation of a fixed budget across chains of decreasing marginal gains. A metric-specific virtual-score transformation followed by a multiway merge, which we call ChainMerge, returns the globally optimal top-$K$ ranking in $O(G+K\log G)$ time from $G$ preordered intent groups, or in $O(n+K\log G)$ time from $n$ globally preordered candidates, instead of the $\Theta(nK)$ of the greedy rule. When intent judgments overlap, exact $\alpha$-DCG optimization is NP-hard under the standard logarithmic discount and $\alpha=0.5$, even when every document has three intents and every intent occurs in two documents. For arbitrary overlap, a polynomial-size LP over nested ranking prefixes upper-bounds the ideal score and certifies the optimality gap of any feasible ranking. In the official TREC Web 2009-2012 judgments, 64.8% of positive documents serve a single intent, yet only 20 of 198 complete queries do so throughout. Beyond this exact regime, the LP certifies 189 of the 198 greedy denominators as globally optimal, and the resulting score intervals preserve the winner in all eight matched comparison groups. On 65,238 MIND-small candidates, ChainMerge returns identical optimal objectives 17-1,011 times faster than the greedy rule. For $\alpha$-DCG, these results trace the hardness of the ideal ranking to intent overlap.

papers.title: Clinical Evidence-Guided Residual Learning for Medication Recommendation with Dynamic DDI Regularization
papers.abstract: Medication recommendation must combine patient-specific treatment evidence with the interaction structure of a prescription. The central challenge is to determine which evidence supports each medication and how strongly to regularize interactions while preserving predictive quality. We propose EviDrug, a clinical evidence-guided residual learning framework. Its clinical-memory backbone integrates a self-trained visit-aware encoder, training-case memory and one medication-set interaction block to establish a patient-specific prescription. A gated refinement head combines the backbone states with clinical associations and history-conditioned medication identities through bounded logit corrections. Drug-drug interaction (DDI) feedback adapts regularization strength using training-query predictions. Across MIMIC-IV, NWICU and SICdb, EviDrug leads twelve published-method baselines in AP, F1 and Jaccard, improving AP by 2.26, 2.06 and 1.71 percentage points over the strongest comparator. These gains come at lower parameter and runtime costs than MetaDrug. Matched controls demonstrate DDI reductions with stable predictive quality. Code is available at https://github.com/LIZESHENG13/EviDrug.

papers.title: Formalizing Patient-Set Semantics for OMOP CDM-Based Clinical Trial Feasibility Assessment:A Neuro-Symbolic Methodology for Traceable Site-Feasibility Patient Counts
papers.abstract: This study examines the interpretation and execution of natural-language eligibility criteria for clinical trial site-feasibility patient-count estimation using the OMOP Common Data Model (CDM). It treats each count as the size of a patient set produced under explicitly declared choices about clinical concepts, temporal conditions, exclusions, proxies, and available data. The study presents NS-CoT, a neuro-symbolic pipeline that uses an LLM to interpret and structure criteria, followed by symbolic processing and deterministic SQL compilation. Intermediate representations and execution records document how criteria are translated into patient sets and counts. Evaluation uses synthetic OMOP CDM data, controlled benchmarks, and a multi-site simulation. Comparisons with a direct-SQL baseline examine execution success, count agreement, patient-set agreement, and preservation of reference-defined site-feasibility labels and rankings. Performance varies across evaluation settings. Layer-wise inspection also supports the identification of implementation and policy errors, followed by correction and re-evaluation. The work investigates the reviewability and fidelity of cohort computation relative to declared reference definitions. It does not establish that these definitions capture a unique clinical ground truth or demonstrate improved recruitment, site selection, or trial outcomes in practice.

papers.title: From User Behaviors to Satisfaction Judgments: Reasoning about User Satisfaction with AI Overviews
papers.abstract: The growing presence of AI overviews in everyday search makes their effective evaluation essential. Response quality has been the primary focus of existing evaluation research, with only a small number of studies examining the user perspective. These evaluations rely on queries and response content, leaving the information conveyed by user behavior insufficiently utilized. This work investigates satisfaction prediction for AI overviews from a user-centered perspective and incorporates behavioral signals into the prediction process. Applying existing behavior-based satisfaction prediction methods from traditional information retrieval to this setting, however, presents limitations. We address these limitations with STaRS, an LLM-based approach designed specifically for predicting satisfaction with AI overviews. At its core is a structured reasoning procedure: individual behavioral signals are interpreted first, and their implications then inform the prediction of user satisfaction. Reinforcement learning further optimizes this procedure, while a reward shaping mechanism alleviates reward sparsity during training. Evaluation on two real-world datasets demonstrates that STaRS outperforms the comparison methods in satisfaction prediction, providing search providers with a practical means of accurately estimating users' satisfaction with AI overviews.
